enquiry: We run a cell culture process in an aqueous medium. Glucose and lactate are measured from samples, and the delay makes it difficult to see changes promptly. We are exploring an in situ spectroscopy pilot that can be checked against those existing laboratory measurements. The medium and cell population change during the run; we have not yet selected a probe or a calibration strategy.

recommendations.rationale: Raman passes the screening for an in-line aqueous application and is the single method whose physics fits an aqueous broth best: it is stated to be well suited to aqueous environments because water absorbs much less than in infrared methods. In the bioprocess section of the same source, Raman is described as usable in the reactor for direct detection of metabolites such as glucose, acetate or lactate, and Raman spectra are stated to support chemometric calibration or classification models. That is a reason to test Raman here, not proof that it will work for this customer's medium, cell line or concentration range.
recommendations.conditions: Only after the fluorescence background of the medium and cells has been checked on real samples, because a fluorescence background can be much stronger than the weak Raman signal. The laser excitation wavelength must be chosen and reported separately from the Raman shift axis. Screening status: pass.

citations.quote: Raman is particularly well-suited for aqueous environments, as it exhibits low absorbance for water molecules compared to infrared methods.
direct detection of specific metabolites like glucose, acetate, or lactate.
Raman spectra (as well as IR absorption spectra) can be used to construct chemometric models-calibration or classification ones.
superposition of luminescence (fluorescence), which has a significantly higher intensity.

recommendations.rationale: Mid-IR ATR passes the screening and is the second single method worth testing against Raman on the same samples. Mid-IR is described as one of the most informative methods of chemical analysis, and ATR fiber probes are described as enabling the analysis of liquids and solid elastic samples, with probe-based analysis in use for in-line, in-process environments. ATR gives an evanescent-wave measurement with a very short effective path, which matters in a water-dominated medium. The comparison tells us which single method carries usable glucose and lactate information in this matrix before any combination is considered.
recommendations.conditions: ATR requires tight contact and suits liquids and soft solids; it samples only a surface layer of a few micrometres, so deposits, fouling and cell adhesion at the crystal are risks, as is sample representativeness in a changing broth. Screening status: pass.

ATR fiber probes (Fig.1) enable the analysis of liquids and solid elastic samples

typically at a depth of few microns
Usable range limited by fiber and crystal; contact, fouling, compatibility.

recommendations.rationale: NIR transmission is conditional: it applies only if the broth stays transparent or semi-transparent throughout the run (Q2). In the dairy example, transmission is the preferred geometry for transparent or semi-transparent liquids, and in the bioprocess section NIR is described as effective for major components such as glucose in the millimolar range. That makes it worth testing as a third single method if - and only if - the optical density allows it. It is not recommended as a first choice for a broth that is or becomes turbid.
recommendations.conditions: Applies only if the broth is and remains transparent or semi-transparent (deciding question Q2: optical density at the start and end of the run). The optical pathlength must be controlled; if it is too wide the signal is lost to absorption, if too narrow the sampled volume is negligible. NIR may lack sensitivity below the trace level stated in the source, so the required glucose and lactate ranges decide its usefulness. Screening status: unknown (Table 1 sample-type fit not confirmed for this sample).

citations.quote: Transmission is the preferred method for transparent or semi-transparent liquids, such as skim milk, whey, or permeate.
the precise control of the optical pathlength (usually 1 - 10 mm); if the pathlength is too wide, the signal is lost to absorption; if too narrow, the sample represents a negligible volume.
NIR spectroscopy is effective for tracking major components like glucose or glycerol in the millimolar range but may lack the sensitivity to detect trace compounds below 0.1 percent.

measurement_concept.probe_and_geometry: In-situ probe in contact with the broth. For Raman: a contact Raman probe with the excitation wavelength stated separately. For mid-IR: an ATR probe immersed in the liquid. For NIR (conditional): a transmission/transflection probe with a controlled optical pathlength, used only while the broth stays transparent or semi-transparent.
measurement_concept.location: In the bioreactor or process line at a point representative of the broth. Medium and cell population change during the run, so the sampling point and the analysed volume matter; ATR analyses only a surface layer of a few micrometres, so contact, deposits and representativeness are risks.
measurement_concept.fiber_link: Fiber link to the spectrometer placed away from the vessel. Silica fibers carry the UV-Vis-NIR range; mid-IR needs chalcogenide (CIR) or polycrystalline (PIR) fibers. The usable fiber length is configuration-dependent; no source states an achievable length for a mid-IR link.

assessment.status_reason: A shortlist of single methods worth testing can be justified from the sources: Raman and mid-IR ATR pass the screening for an in-line aqueous application, and NIR transmission is conditional on the broth's optical density. The concentration ranges, required accuracy and required response time are not known, so this is a provisional assessment with stated assumptions, not a selection of a probe or a calibration strategy. Any combination is only a later hypothesis to test against the best single method.

clarification_questions.question: What are the typical and extreme glucose and lactate concentrations in the broth, what accuracy and precision do you need, and what response time (update interval) would let you act on the result?
clarification_questions.why_it_matters: These numbers are the basis for the go/no-go criteria and decide whether a method with lower sensitivity for trace levels can be used at all.

clarification_questions.question: How turbid is the broth at the start and at the end of the run (optical density), and does it stay transparent or semi-transparent?
clarification_questions.why_it_matters: Transmission geometry only works while light can pass through the sample; turbidity decides between transmission, ATR and reflection geometry, and therefore the technique.

clarification_questions.question: Does the medium or the cell population show a strong fluorescence background, and can we measure a representative sample to check it?
clarification_questions.why_it_matters: A strong fluorescence background can mask the weak Raman signal, which would change the method ranking.

recommendations.rationale: Raman passes the screening for an in-line aqueous application and is the single method whose physics fits an aqueous broth best: it is stated to be well suited to aqueous environments because water absorbs much less than in infrared methods. In the bioprocess section of the same source, Raman is described as usable in the reactor for direct detection of metabolites such as glucose, acetate or lactate, and Raman spectra are stated to support chemometric calibration or classification models. That is a reason to test Raman here, not proof that it will work for this customer's medium, cell line or concentration range.
recommendations.conditions: Only after the fluorescence background of the medium and cells has been checked on real samples, because a fluorescence background can be much stronger than the weak Raman signal. The laser excitation wavelength must be chosen and reported separately from the Raman shift axis. Screening status: pass.

citations.quote: Raman is particularly well-suited for aqueous environments, as it exhibits low absorbance for water molecules compared to infrared methods.
direct detection of specific metabolites like glucose, acetate, or lactate.
Raman spectra (as well as IR absorption spectra) can be used to construct chemometric models-calibration or classification ones.
superposition of luminescence (fluorescence), which has a significantly higher intensity.

recommendations.rationale: Mid-IR ATR passes the screening and is the second single method worth testing against Raman on the same samples. Mid-IR is described as one of the most informative methods of chemical analysis, and ATR fiber probes are described as enabling the analysis of liquids and solid elastic samples, with probe-based analysis in use for in-line, in-process environments. ATR gives an evanescent-wave measurement with a very short effective path, which matters in a water-dominated medium. The comparison tells us which single method carries usable glucose and lactate information in this matrix before any combination is considered.
recommendations.conditions: ATR requires tight contact and suits liquids and soft solids; it samples only a surface layer of a few micrometres, so deposits, fouling and cell adhesion at the crystal are risks, as is sample representativeness in a changing broth. Screening status: pass.

recommendations.rationale: NIR transmission is conditional: it applies only if the broth stays transparent or semi-transparent throughout the run (Q2). In the dairy example, transmission is the preferred geometry for transparent or semi-transparent liquids, and in the bioprocess section NIR is described as effective for major components such as glucose in the millimolar range. That makes it worth testing as a third single method if - and only if - the optical density allows it. It is not recommended as a first choice for a broth that is or becomes turbid.
recommendations.conditions: Applies only if the broth is and remains transparent or semi-transparent (deciding question Q2: optical density at the start and end of the run). The optical pathlength must be controlled; if it is too wide the signal is lost to absorption, if too narrow the sampled volume is negligible. NIR may lack sensitivity below the trace level stated in the source, so the required glucose and lactate ranges decide its usefulness. Screening status: unknown (Table 1 sample-type fit not confirmed for this sample).

the precise control of the optical pathlength (usually 1 - 10 mm); if the pathlength is too wide, the signal is lost to absorption; if too narrow, the sample represents a negligible volume.

measurement_concept.probe_and_geometry: In-situ probe in contact with the broth. For Raman: a contact Raman probe with the excitation wavelength stated separately. For mid-IR: an ATR probe immersed in the liquid. For NIR (conditional): a transmission/transflection probe with a controlled optical pathlength, used only while the broth stays transparent or semi-transparent.
measurement_concept.location: In the bioreactor or process line at a point representative of the broth. Medium and cell population change during the run, so the sampling point and the analysed volume matter; ATR analyses only a surface layer of a few micrometres, so contact, deposits and representativeness are risks.
measurement_concept.fiber_link: Fiber link to the spectrometer placed away from the vessel. Silica fibers carry the UV-Vis-NIR range; mid-IR needs chalcogenide (CIR) or polycrystalline (PIR) fibers. The usable fiber length is configuration-dependent; no source states an achievable length for a mid-IR link.
